title: An f32 as an exact C literal
starter:
import math


def c_float(x: float) -> str:
    """x is already an f32 value (held in a Python float). Return C source that
    produces exactly x: NAN for any nan, INFINITY, (-INFINITY), and otherwise
    the shortest exact hex float with an f suffix: 1.0 -> "0x1p+0f"."""
    return f"{x:g}f"
hints: Handle the three special values first. Use `math.isnan(x)`, because `x == float('nan')` is always False. Then `math.isinf(x)` and the sign of `x`.
Split `x.hex()` at `'p'`. Strip `'0'` from the right of the left part, then strip a leftover `'.'`, and glue `'p'`, the exponent, and `'f'` back on.

Why `(-INFINITY)` with parentheses: the literal lands inside bigger C expressions, and a leading minus can merge with an operator printed just before it (`x--INFINITY` lexes as `x-- INFINITY`). Negative finite literals have the same risk, so parenthesize those in your renderer too, or always put spaces around operators.
prompt:
Write c_float(x). The input is already an f32 value held in a Python float. Return NAN for any NaN, INFINITY for +inf, (-INFINITY) for -inf, and otherwise the exact hex float in its shortest form, followed by f. So 1.0 gives 0x1p+0f and -2.5 gives -0x1.4p+1f.

x.hex() prints the exact bits, but always with 13 fraction digits, like 0x1.4000000000000p+1. Drop the trailing zeros of the fraction, and the dot too if nothing is left after it.

answer.explain: A hex float names the exact binary value, so it can't be misread the way a short decimal can (`%g` turns FLT_MAX into 3.40282e+38, which reads back as a different float). The solution special-cases NaN (with either sign) and the infinities, which have no numeric literal. Everything else is `x.hex()` with the padding zeros trimmed, plus `f`, including -0.0 as `-0x0p+0f`.
